Learning Objectives
Define the extracellular matrix building blocks of musculoskeletal tissues.
Examine the composition and structure of the extracellular matrix, and determine how the
extracellular matrix dictates tissue biomechanical behavior.
Outline extracellular matrix remodeling.
Identify biologic functions of the extracellular matrix.
Extracellular Matrix Building Blocks
Collagens are the most abundant proteins in the musculoskeletal system. More than 30
collagen types exist, and they generally can be categorized as fibrillar or nonfibrillar. The most

abundant fibrillar collagens are type I (found in tendon and bone) and type II (found in
articular cartilage).1
Collagen is very stable and has limited turnover under non-pathologic conditions.2
Proteoglycans are the second most abundant proteins in the musculoskeletal system. They
consist of core proteins with one or more attached glycosaminoglycans. Cartilaginous tissues
are rich in the large proteoglycan aggrecan3 (Resource 1). Connective tissues, such as tendon,
contain the small proteoglycans decorin and biglycan4 (Resource 2).
Mineral makes up approximately 70% (by mass) of bone. Bone mineral is a carbonated
hydroxyapatite5 (Resource 3).

Extracellular Matrix Building Blocks
The basic extracellular building blocks for the musculoskeletal system are collagens,
proteoglycans, and bone mineral. Depending on the functional requirement of the
tissue, the types and ratios of these building blocks vary. For example, high levels of
mineral in bone provide structural stiffness, high levels of proteoglycans in articular
cartilage provide resistance to compression, and dense bundles of collagen in tendon
provide resistance to tension. Fibrocartilage contains a mix of cartilage-like matrix and
tendon-line matrix to resist the mixed compressive and tensile loads to which it is
subjected.
Collagen Fibrillogenesis
For fibril-forming collagens, triple-helix molecules (300 nm in length, 1.5 nm in diameter) are
extruded from cells into the extracellular space and self-assemble into larger fibrillar
structures.5
Microfibrils are an assemblage of five strands of stacked collagen molecules. Within each
strand, the collagen is stacked with an approximately 36-nm gap space between the N-
terminus of one collagen molecule and the C-terminus of the succeeding molecule. The five
strands are staggered (along their stacking direction) with respect to each other by
approximately 67 nm (approximately one-fourth the length of a collagen molecule and,
therefore, termed quarter-staggered).6

Collagen molecules are cross-linked via the enzyme lysyl oxidase.

Collagen Fibrillogenesis
Collagen fibrillogenesis is a self-assembly process that occurs in the extracellular space.
Collagen molecules pack in a well-ordered, quarter-staggered arrangement to produce
multiple hierarchies of organization from the molecular to the tissue length scales.

Cell Biology of the Extracellular Matrix
The extracellular matrix (ECM) is formed and maintained by resident tissue cells.
Osteoblasts in bone produce and mineralize type I collagen.
Chondrocytes in articular cartilage produce type II collagen and proteoglycan.
Tenocytes in tendon produce type I collagen.
Remodeling of the ECM in unmineralized tissues is achieved via a collection of enzymes called
metalloproteinases (MMPs).
Remodeling of bone ECM is achieved via osteoclast-mediated resorption of bone followed by
osteoblast formation of new bone.

Cell Biology of the Extracellular Matrix
Musculoskeletal stromal cells form and remodel the ECM of musculoskeletal tissues.
These cells produce, orient, cross-link, and mineralize the appropriate mix of ECM
building blocks to address the functional needs of each tissue. The matrix is maintained
via regular remodeling. Collagen and proteoglycans are degraded by MMPs. Each MMP
can degrading a specific set of proteins. For example, collagenases (eg, MMP1) cleave
fibrillar collagens. Mineralized matrix is remodeled via MMP-driven degradation of
collagen and acid-driven dissolution of mineral.
Structural Arrangement of the Extracellular Matrix
ECM proteins are arranged to accommodate the functional requirement of the tissue.
In bone, mineral is arranged within and around collagen fibrils to achieve a high bending
modulus.

In cartilage, collagen and proteoglycan molecules form a network that achieves a high
compressive modulus via a balance of fluid pressurization and matrix stiffness.
In tendon, densely packed collagen fibers are aligned in the direction of muscle force to
achieve a high tensile modulus.

Structural Arrangement of the Extracellular Matrix
The mechanical properties of musculoskeletal tissues are derived from the composition
and structural arrangement of extracellular protein. A small number of basic ECM
building blocks are combined at various ratios and arrangements to produce a wide
range of mechanical behavior, including high bending stiffness (eg, bone), high
compressive modulus (eg, cartilage), and high tensile strength (eg, tendon).
Bone ECM
Composition and Structure
Bone ECM primarily consists of organic type I collagen (approximately 30% by mass) and
inorganic hydroxyapatite mineral (approximately 70% by mass)5,7 (Figure 2; Table 1; Resource
4).
Approximately 90% of the organic component in bone is type I collagen and approximately
10% consists of proteoglycans and non-collagenous proteins.
Mineralization occurs on nucleation sites in gap regions and surfaces of collagen fibrils.
Mineral crystals begin to form from the necessary ions, particularly calcium and phosphate,
that come together to form a nucleus and initiate crystallization.
Bone mineral contains soluble impurities (eg, carbonate, magnesium), allowing it to serve as a
reservoir for calcium, phosphate, and magnesium.
Mutations in type I collagen may result in considerable bone disorders, such as osteogenesis
imperfecta.


Composition and Structure
Bone is primarily composed of type I collagen and hydroxyapatite mineral. The collagen
matrix serves as a template onto which mineral crystals nucleate and grow. Minerals fill
the gap spaces and coat the surfaces of collagen fibrils. Mineral makes up approximately
50% of the volume (approximately 70% of the mass) and collagen makes up
approximately 50% of the volume (approximately 30% of the mass) of bone. Bone
mineral is a carbonated hydroxyapatite that forms nanometer-sized, plate-shaped
crystals.
Biomechanics
The biomechanics of bone are defined by its structure (mass and architecture) and by its
composition (the bone matrix).

The fibrous (collagen) matrix dictates the tensile properties and fracture toughness of bone;
the mineral phase dictates the stiffness and compressive strength of bone.
The nature of the mineral crystals is important for the mechanical properties of bone.
Crystallinity (including crystal size, shape, and perfection), which changes with age, is
associated with ultimate strain and toughness.
The nature of collagen fibril cross-linking also is important for bone’s mechanical properties.
Cross-links likely contribute to bone toughness, dissipating energy in the tissue if they rupture
under loading.
Bone biomechanics typically are determined by deforming the bone (eg, in three-point
bending) and measuring the load. The resulting load-deformation curve defines the strength,
stiffness, ductility (ability to deform), and energy to fracture of bone. Adjusting for the
geometry of bone, the resulting stress-strain curve defines the intrinsic properties of the
tissue, including ultimate stress, modulus of elasticity, and modulus of toughness (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Graphs show force-displacement (A) and stress-strain (B) curves for bone. In panel A,
applied load is plotted as a function of displacement. Important properties related to strength,
stiffness, ductility or ability to deform, and ability to dissipate energy can be derived from this
curve. This characteristic graph represents the structural behavior of a sample and is
influenced by the size and shape of the sample and its material properties. By normalizing for
the geometry of the sample, a complimentary stress-strain curve is obtained (B). Similar
information can be calculated from this curve, but these parameters are estimated material
properties that are no longer dependent on size and shape. Note the yield point at which

use the 0.2% offset method in the stress-strain domain as shown. (Reproduced from Burr DB,


Biomechanics
The biomechanics of bone depend on the amounts and arrangement of its primary
compositional components: fibrillar type I collagen and carbonated hydroxyapatite
mineral. Relative to unmineralized tissues, such as tendon and cartilage, bone has high
stiffness and compressive strength; however, it maintains a high level of toughness,
derived from its extensible collagen matrix. The balance between high stiffness (from
minerals) and high toughness (from collagen) results in a resilient tissue that functions to
mechanically stabilize the skeleton under many cycles of load during physiologic
activities.
ECM Remodeling
Bone contains four distinct cell types: osteoblasts, osteoclasts, osteocytes, and bone lining
cells. These cells maintain bone through anabolic or catabolic functions.
Osteocytes and osteoblasts synthesize and secrete the organic components (primarily type I
collagen) of bone and control its mineralization.
Osteoclasts resorb bone via enzymatic degradation of collagen and acid-based dissolution of
mineral.
Osteocytes and lining cells are resident cells that maintain the matrix and respond to
mechanical signals.

ECM Remodeling
Bone is maintained via a remodeling process controlled by osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and
osteocytes. Osteoblasts are the primary bone-forming cell, producing and mineralizing
collagen matrix. Osteocytes are former osteoblasts embedded in bone matrix that
transduce mechanical signals and induce bone remodeling if necessary. Osteoclasts are

Water is the most abundant component of articular cartilage, representing 65% to 80% of its

The ECM of articular cartilage consists of collagen (10% to 20% of wet weight) and
proteoglycans (10% to 15% of wet weight; Table 2). The primary collagen is type II (90%), and
the primary proteoglycan is aggrecan (95%; Figure 4).

The hydrophilic nature of proteoglycans gives cartilage its affinity for water.
Chondrocytes make up approximately 1% to 5% of the volume of cartilage and maintain the
ECM. Chondrocytes are surrounded by a nest-like pericellular matrix made up of type V
collagen.
Alignment of collagen fiber in articular cartilage varies with the depth of the tissue. Fibers on
the surface zone (top 10%) are aligned tangential to the surface, fibers in the middle zone (40%
to 60%) are randomly aligned, and fibers in the deep zone (30%) are aligned perpendicular to
(and insert into) the bone (Figure 5).
The tidemark is a boundary between the calcified and uncalcified layers of articular cartilage.
Mutations in type II collagen may lead to several cartilage diseases (eg, Stickler syndrome and
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease).

Composition and Structure
Cartilage is a composite of water, collagen fibrils, and proteoglycans. The collagen fibers
and hydrophilic proteoglycans are tightly packed and retain hydration in the tissue.
Chondrocytes sparsely populate the cartilage and maintain the ECM. Composition and

lubrication and tensile strength at the surface zone, compressive properties in the
middle zone, and anchoring to the bone in the deep zone.
Biomechanics
Cartilage provides a low-friction articulating surface and supports high compressive loads
across the joint8 (Resource 5).
Cartilage compressive behavior classically has been described by the biphasic theory, which
considers the tissue as two phases: solid and fluid. Time-varying (viscoelastic) behavior is
dictated by fluid flow in and out of the cartilage. Elastic behavior is dictated by the properties
of the solid matrix. If cartilage is mechanically loaded, the interstitial fluid in the tissue
pressurizes and flows from high pressure (loaded) to low pressure (unloaded) regions. At the
time of contact, the fluid is pressurized and carries the stress. Over time, fluid flows out of the
cartilage, and stress is transferred from the fluid to the solid. At equilibrium, all stress is
carried by the solid matrix.
The resistance to fluid flow is defined by the so-called permeability of cartilage, which largely is
determined by the proteoglycan content of tissue.
In the surface zone, the tangential orientation of the collagen fibers provides tensile strength
to resist osmotic swelling in the underlying cartilage.
Cartilage biomechanics typically are determined by compressing cartilage samples in confined
or unconfined compression. For viscoelastic tests, the resulting stress relaxation or creep
curves are used to define the cartilage permeability and aggregate modulus.
The low-friction characteristics of cartilage partly result from the lubricating characteristics of
synovial fluid and hyaluronic acid. If contact area is reduced, interstitial fluid pressurization
drastically reduces the frictional coefficient of cartilage-cartilage sliding.

Biomechanics
Articular cartilage has remarkable frictional and compressive mechanical properties.
Despite more than a million cycles of loading per year and limited remodeling, cartilage
is resilient for many decades. The basis for this mechanical function is the interplay
between its compositional makeup: collagen fibers, proteoglycans, and water.SEND FEEDBACK

Particularly, fluid pressurization plays a critical role, reducing contact area and friction at
the surface and supporting compressive stress at the instant of contact.
ECM Remodeling
Cartilage demonstrates minimal remodeling and matrix turnover, which limits the ability of
cartilage to maintain and/or repair its ECM.
Cell numbers, proteoglycan synthesis, and water content decrease with age.
Proteoglycan loss is characteristic of osteoarthritis, leading to progressive loss of mechanical
properties.

ECM Remodeling
Because of a paucity of cells and limited remodeling activity, cartilage is unable to
prevent or repair damage to its matrix. This predisposes the tissue to age- and injury-
related degeneration. Loss of critical ECM components, such as aggrecan leads to a
decreased compressive modulus and increased permeability.
Tendon and Ligament ECM
Composition and Structure
Tendons are dense connective tissues that attach muscle to bone. Ligaments are dense
connective tissues that attach bone to bone.3
Water makes up 50% to 70% of tendon/ligament wet weight.
Tendon is populated by fibroblast-like cells called tenocytes, or tendon fibroblasts. Ligament is
populated by fibroblast-like cells called ligamentocytes, or ligament fibroblasts.
The primary ECM component in tendon is collagen, which makes up more than 75% of the dry
weight of tissue. In tendon, 95% of the collagen is type I, with most of the remaining collagen
being type III. The second major ECM component is the small, leucine-rich proteoglycan. The
two most abundant proteoglycans in tendon are decorin and biglycan.

The ECM of ligament is similar to that of tendon. Collagen makes up more than 70% of the dry
weight of tissue. In ligament, 90% of the collagen is type I, and the remaining collagen is type
III. Proteoglycans make up a small percentage of the ECM of ligament. Distinct from tendon,
ligament matrix is approximately 1% elastin.
Tendon structure is hierarchical: triple-helix collagen molecules combine to form microfibrils,
which combine to form fibrils, then fascicles, and ultimately the tendon itself (Figure 6).
Ligament has a similar hierarchical structure.
Mutations in ECM components may result in considerable connective tissue diseases (eg,
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome).

molecules assembled into progressively larger bundles until the level of the tendon itself is
reached. Note the endotenon (surrounding the fascicle) and the epitenon (surrounding the

Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp
215-230.)

Composition and Structure
Tendons and ligaments have a similar ECM composition and structural organization.
Both tissues have a fibrillar hierarchical structure of densely packed collagen that forms
rope-like tissue structures. Besides collagen, which makes up most of the tissue dry

Biomechanics
Tendon biomechanical functions
Transfer muscle-generated load to bone to actuate joint motion
Store and elastically transfer energy (eg, the Achilles tendon)
Precisely position a joint (eg, the flexor tendons of the hand)
Ligament functions
Static stabilization of the joint
Load sharing across the joint
The highly aligned collagen fibers in tendon and ligament are oriented according to their
required function. Tendon fibers are aligned in the direction of the muscle force line of action.
Ligament fibers are generally less aligned than tendons to account for tensile and torsional
loads to which they are subjected (Figure 7).
Tendon collagen fibers display a crimped structure, which is associated with nonlinear
mechanical behavior at low loads (Figure 8).

The role of minor extracellular components in tendons and ligaments is a subject of debate.
Dissimilar from cartilage, it is unclear if there is a biomechanical role for proteoglycans in
tendon/ligament; however, a clear role for proteoglycans in controlling collagen fibrillogenesis
and tissue formation has been described.9 Elastin, found in ligaments, is thought to improve
tissue elasticity by assisting in returning a loaded tissue to its prestretched length.
Tendon and ligament biomechanics typically are determined by pulling samples in tension.
The resulting load-deformation curve defines the strength, stiffness, and energy to fracture of
the tissue. If adjusting for the geometry of the tendon, the resulting stress-strain curve defines
the intrinsic properties of the tissue, including ultimate stress, modulus of elasticity, and
modulus of toughness. For viscoelasticity, stress relaxation and creep curves are used to
determine tissue elastic modulus and time constants (Figure 9).

Biomechanics
The fibrillar hierarchical structure of tendons and ligaments results in a high tensile
modulus. Tendon collagen fibers are aligned with the direction of muscle force to
transfer load to bone and cause joint motion. Ligament collagen fibers are aligned
according to the stabilizing requirement of a particular ligament (eg, the anterior cruciate
ligament is oriented to prevent anterior tibial translation).

The fibroblast-like cells in tendon and ligament maintain and remodel the matrix as necessary

Tendon and ligament are responsive to their loading environment. Immobilization leads to
degradation of tissue and decreases its tensile strength, total weight, cellularity, collagen
organization, and collagen fibril diameters. Conversely, exercise leads to increased turnover of
collagen, including synthesis and degradation, with a net increase in synthesis.

Dissimilar from cartilage, which demonstrates limited ECM remodeling, the fibroblasts in
tendon and ligament are responsive to their environment and capable of degrading and
synthesizing local matrix.
Fibrocartilage ECM
Intervertebral Disk Composition, Structure, and Biomechanics
The intervertebral disk (IVD) is a fibrocartilaginous tissue that supports compressive loads and
allows for motion between vertebral bodies10 (Resource 6).
The IVD consists of two structures: an inner cartilaginous nucleus pulposus and an outer
fibrous anulus fibrosus. The ECM composition of the nucleus pulposus resembles cartilage:
77% water, 14% proteoglycan, and 4% collagen. The ECM of the anulus fibrosus resembles
tendon: 60% water, 5% proteoglycan, and 15% collagen11-28 (Table 3).

The major proteoglycan in the IVD is aggrecan, found primarily in the nucleus pulposus. Similar

Meniscus and Labrum Composition, Structure, and Biomechanics
The meniscus in the knee and the labrum in the shoulder are analogous fibrocartilage
structures that decrease contact stresses in, distribute load across, and stabilize the joints
(Resource 7).
The cell type populating the meniscus and labrum is the fibrochondrocyte, which produces
tendon-like (eg, type I collagen) and cartilage-like (eg, aggrecan) ECM.
Water accounts for 65% to 75% of the weight and volume of the meniscus. Collagen, primarily
type I, makes up 75% of the dry weight of the meniscus and provides tensile strength. Other
extracellular proteins, such as proteoglycans, make up approximately 10% of the dry weight of
the meniscus.
The meniscus displays regional variation in cell phenotype, vascularity, and ECM composition.
The inner third of the meniscus is avascular and cartilaginous in matrix and cell phenotype; the
outer third is vascularized and more fibrillar in makeup (Figure 11).
Collagen fibers are disorganized in the superficial layer of the meniscus. In the deeper layers,
collagen fibers, which are bound together by radially oriented tie fibers, run circumferentially.
This structure is comparable to that of the anulus fibrosus in the IVD and functions similarly,
converting compressive forces in the knee to circumferential hoop stresses.
Although less studied, the labrum displays similar features in ECM composition and
biomechanical function to the meniscus.

Enthesis Composition, Structure, and Biomechanics
Attachment of a compliant material, such as tendon (with a modulus on the order of 200 MPa),
to a relatively stiff material, such as bone (with a modulus on the order of 20 GPa), poses a
difficult mechanical challenge.11
The tendon enthesis possesses a transitional fibrocartilagenous region between soft tissue
and bone that exhibits gradations in cell phenotype, matrix composition, tissue organization,
and mechanical properties. Entheses are found at the bony attachments of tendons,
ligaments, menisci, and other connective tissues (Figure 12).

The compositional gradient of the enthesis shifts from tendon-like (type I collagen, decorin,
biglycan) to cartilage-like (type II collagen, aggrecan) to mineralized cartilage (type X collagen,
hydroxyapatite mineral) to bone-like (type I collagen, hydroxyapatite mineral).
These gradations facilitate the transfer of load between the two materials by reducing
potentially damaging stress concentrations that would otherwise arise at their interface.

Fibrocartilage tissues are composed of a wide range of ECM proteins, combining
features of tendon, cartilage, and bone. Depending on the biomechanical requirements
of the tissue, the matrix may contain different levels of fibrillar collagen (providing
tensile strength), proteoglycans (providing compressive properties), and/or mineral
(providing stiffening).

Bone contains almost all the calcium in the body; this element is essential for a wide range of
biologic processes (eg, muscle function, cellular mechanotransduction, nerve
transmission).12 (Resource 8)
Hydroxyapatite mineral is the primary store of calcium in bone.
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is produced if the concentration of calcium in blood drops below
a threshold level. PTH triggers the release of calcium from bone ECM (Figure 13).
PTH also promotes the absorption of calcium directly, by increasing calcium reabsorption by
the kidneys, and indirectly, by stimulating vitamin D activity.
The hormone calcitonin, produced by the thyroid gland, also regulates calcium in the blood
by opposing the action of PTH.

The ECM as a growth factor repository
Several growth factors are stored in the ECM, often in latent form, and released if necessary.
Growth factors that bind to the ECM, particularly heparin sulfate proteoglycans, include
fibroblast growth factors, transforming growth factors, bone morphogenetic proteins,
wingless-related integration site factors, and vascular endothelial growth factors.

Theories on why growth factors are stored in the ECM include that they serve as reservoirs
for rapid release after injury and as spatial gradients for developmental patterning.
Growth-factor release from the ECM is dictated by MMPs. Local cells produce these enzymes
to cleave the matrix and release a specific growth factor for a desired biologic function.
The ECM as a progenitor cell niche
Recently, the ECM has been revealed as a crucial niche for tissue-specific progenitor cell
maintenance and renewal.
Connective tissue progenitor cells have been identified in numerous musculoskeletal tissues,
including bone and tendon. These cells reside in ECM niches within the tissues.
The bone marrow cavity houses hematopoietic stem cells adjacent to osteoblasts. These two
cell types interact to produce hematopoietic stem-cell–activating proteins. The bone marrow
also houses mesenchymal stem cells, which can give rise to cartilage and bone and repair or
regenerate injured tissues (Figure 14).
Connective tissues, such as tendon and ligament, contain tissue-specific progenitor cells,
typically found in the perivascular niche, which provide a source of cells for repair.
